name: Bishr ibn Abi Khazim
bio: Bishr ibn Abi Khazim of Asad was, in Lyall's words, the most considerable poet of his tribe during the century before the Prophet. He was a contemporary of Hatim of Tayyi', of an-Nabighah of Dhubyan and of King an-Nu'man Abu Qabus.
Lyall mentions the battle of an-Nisar, about A.D. 575, as a point of time in his career.

poems.title: Ode XCVI: Ramah and its hill no longer
poems.author: Bishr ibn Abi Khazim
poems.note: Lyall's heading: Bishr son of Abu Khazim, of Walibah, of Asad.
poems.text:
Ramah and its hill no longer bear traces of Sulaima, and her journeyings and their divergencies have carried her far away from thee ;

There has changed her that which has changed men before her : she is gone, and the longings of my heart seek her out.

Has it not reached her that tears flow ceaselessly from an eye whose Beloved visits it only in dreams —

[Dropping] like the dripping of well-water from [the labour of] a camel of Jurash over seed-beds, whose great water-skins gush forth into the channels—

[A camel] drawing a great water-bag by a rope of four strands over a cross-piece, kept straight by a pulley with suspending irons the orifices of which creak as it works?

She went by the upland road — no other objective had she than Muhajjar and the Harrah of Laila, its level spaces and its black lava rocks.

She saw me with my temples bald and smooth as the place where the sand-grouse lays : but their baldness is not due to a captor who showed grace in view of ransom to be paid having cut away the locks.

We answered the sons of Sa'd of Dabbah when they called to us for help : and a wonderful friend were he who when called on did not answer !

It came about that, whenever we cried ' Hawazin, advance in the straight road ! ' — their orator hit not the mark aright.

From al-Mala we gripped them with the grip of the biting she-camel, with a gleaming [body of horse] the scouts of which do not walk under coverts ;

And when they saw us in an-Nisar as though we were high-reaching clouds brought by the Pleiades, driven on before the south-wind,

Then were they like a woman boiling cream in a pot who, when it boils up, knows not what to do, whether to take it off the fire [before it is cooked] and so incur blame, or to let the butter be melted [and thus perhaps be lost].

We cut their forces in twain — one half was in al-Yamamah, while the other took the way of Autas, where their dogs howled [at their strange surroundings].

We drove them as we would from place to place, as bitches carry about their puppies, on every track stretching like a scar in the desert, with its dust rising high in air.

We stripped the bark off them as a man peels staves, and they reached a state in which the despoiled one whimpers over his misery—

From early morning until the night came between us and them, and weariness overtook the running of our most enduring steeds.

Our cavalry singled out Qushair, and went straight for them, as the well straightens out the ropes of the buckets that ply therein.

Whensoever we overtook any band of their horsemen, we remembered their rancour and their wrongs done against us, [and dealt bloodily with them] !

Ye Sons of 'Amir! ye know how we left your women — snatched off captive in haste, with their hinder-parts bleeding [from the roughness of the cushion-less saddles] :

Yea, our sutlers and hirelings had their will with white women fair as statues, with their bosoms perfumed with saffron.

Your suckling women passed the night [hid away] on a hill, with their hearts trembling with fear of that which the darkness might hide.

Leave alone the pastures of the Shlqani ! both of them belong to us, what time wars blaze up among Red Mudar !

poems.title: Ode XCVII: Ah, gone on her way is
poems.author: Bishr ibn Abi Khazim
poems.note: Lyall's heading: The same. Lyall: the ode has two inconsistent openings; the alternative opening couplet is given in his notes and is not reproduced here.
poems.text:
Ah, gone on her way is Idam ; and every tie to a fair one must one day wear out and snap !

Thou hast been her lover in earnest and in jest, until now that thou hast grown old, and men say — ' Verily thou art distraught ! '

Once was she well content with us for a space, and we with her : but time has no abiding !

The nights when she took thee captive with her rows of pearly teeth, whose moisture, when a third of the night had sped, was potent as heady wine,

And a bright face with shining cheeks, sleek, and a nose on and about which beauty had been showered.

[She turns her head aside] as turns an antelope with hard smooth horn, that has been left behind by the herd, in Sahah, where the acacia-trees line its moist ravines,

Her companion a fawn, brownish in colour, with languishing eyes — its bleating disquiets her motherly heart.

Yea, many the wide desert where the drumming of the Jinn resounds, and in its waterless spaces the hot wind whistles shrilly,

Where I have startled its gazelles as they took their mid-day rest, what time the hills pierced through the glistening stretches of the mirage,

Mounted on a fleet she-camel whose frame has been worn down by constant journeyings until I have reached to her ultimate nature, and her hump has vanished away.

She is like a flat-nosed wild bull that roams from one region to another, over whom has passed, in Harbah, a night set thick with rainclouds :

He stood night-long, crying ' Turn to morning, O Night ' ! till the dark-ness cleared away from his strip of sand,

And he emerged therefrom in the early dawn, as a pearl shows forth when let fall from the string.

Ho ! carry a message to the Sons of Sa'd and to their cousin — the last drops in the udder have been drawn !

' We offer you the way of uprightness : and we are a people whose affection if one quits, he will have no praise in war.

' Then, since your vessels of love are empty, and there is not in them any tie between us of mutual affection and aid,

' Therefore the valley-sides of 'Uraitinat and the gravelly plain of 'Aiham are forbidden to you.

' We will close them against you, though they be lands wherein the flanks and humps of the camels grow fat and swell :

' There the eyes of men's milch-camels are well content, and the clouds untie thereon the spouts of their water-bags.'

Yea, many the rich pasture from which the seekers for grazing refrain in fear, wherein grow luxuriantly the nafal and the JiaudMn, —

Its greenery rises high and is tangled together, and the places where the 'alajan grows stand out in it like moles—

Have we made free with for the use of a tribe great in multitude : when their herds are beset with an alarm, they [flee not, but] stand and defend them.

The meeting-place of council cannot hold them all : they must part into companies wheresoever they make a halt ;

Their men have no need to run afoot : they have spare horses in plenty standing ready bridled —

Steeds that stood the whole night and the first part of the day at al-Mimha, where thagham was cut for their fodder.

Then, when they came down into the plain from Dhu Sabah, and the torrent-beds and the hills streamed with them,

They stirred up a cloud of dust and emerged therefrom, as the arrows pierce through and come forth from the target.

In every place of soft soil where they wheeled about is a well-like foot-print of the hoof, with the sides crumbling in.

When the foremost of them emerge, dishevelled, rushing headlong with their forelocks standing out,

With bundles of mail-coats bound to their cruppers, with their colts in the evening looking [, with their long thin legs,] like pairs of shears,

Then do they race with the spear-heads, bending downwards their heads, as doves race with one another as they fly towards the scanty pools left by the rain.

Seest thou not that length of time brings forgetfulness and oblivion, even as Judham is forgotten ?

They were of our tribe, but wrought wrong against us : and we led them forth to the country of the Syrians.

We had been in defence of them a strong fortress : ours was the supreme headship and the foremost place.

And they said to us — ' Ye cannot abide where ye are if we go forth from you ' : yet we abode in our place though they had gone —

Stone blocks of Khuzaimah, firmly fixed in the soil : to us belong the ways through the mountains, whether free or forbidden.

And sooth, the day when we stood up to curse you in the valley of Dhu-l-Majaz shall bring its fruit in your punishment !

poems.title: Ode XCVIII: Ah, our partners have departed and
poems.author: Bishr ibn Abi Khazim
poems.text:
Ah, our partners have departed and cannot be reached, and thy heart is in the keeping of the ladies as they journey away !

The drivers make their way with them towards the waters of Nakhl, and they turn aside from the twin peaks of Aban.

I question my companion — and yet I think that I can myself see clearly whither the ladies are taking their way :

I fear lest the Sons of 'Uqail should depart with my Beloved one : and verily justified is fear !

Therefore hardly did I turn my eyes away from them in Qaniyah, what time the day had risen high.

In the night they came upon Arum and Shabah, with Ti'ar to the left thereof:

In the litters were girls like gazelles of Asnumah resting in their holes, the coverts too short to hide them fully.

As they smile, their lips part to show a row of camomile-flowers, washed bright by rain after a night-travelling cloud has passed over them.

And among the dames in the litters is one kind and playful, whose people are making for their own land and have started on their way—

One of those nurtured far from all hardship ; her dwelling-places have been al-Qasimah and al-Uwar ;

Her diet is milk slightly soured, flowing to her in abundance, and pure milk what time the milch-camels are sent forth [to bring in grain] ;

She is plump where the anklets go round, soft and tender, and in her flanks and belly is slenderness ;

Heavy are her after-parts whenever she essays to rise, and when she hastens, she is soon out of breath.

Then I passed the night wakeful, without sleep, as though strong wine were coursing through my joints,

Watching in the heavens the Bearers of the Bier, as they revolve like the moving on of a herd of wild kine ;

And the Pleiads incline to setting after the first part of night is spent, while Capella stands out as their neighbour.

Help, O ye people, for the man oppressed with misery by the slow length of Time, for his durance has lasted long !

Yea, if distant regions have taken away from us the fair ones of 'Uqail, and the hearts which they carry away captive with them,

Yet, until War turned us away one from the other, we and they had aforetime many days together that were but too short—

The nights when I paid no heed to him that would hold me back, and my waist-wrapper flowed down over my ankles,

And I disobeyed him that chid me, and I achieved delight, and vexed, by my visits, one stirred by jealousy.

But when we saw that the men had become our enemies, with no opening left to agreement between them [and us],

Our vanguard moved on, until we pitched camp in a land which Nizar had placed under a ban among themselves ;

And Tayyi' of the twin mountains kindled a war from the pain of which distant Suhar shrieked out.

They blocked the passes when they saw us coming : but creeping into their burrows did not save them from us.

And the tribe, the tribe of the sons of Subai', dwelt in Quradiyah, and we encompassed them about in a ring ;

And 'Amr son of 'Amr counselled his people not to fight — like a man who should cut off his own nose while he had still power to defend himself :

At Dhat Kahf they offered peace : but the taste of it to them is as bitter as sola' or pitch.

And the Ribab fled away to the Upland, and there remained not of them in Sarat or al-Hubs a single fire ;

Then they kept at a distance from us, though in sooth they thought us near, in a place where secret talk could be overheard.

[And fear of us brought Sa'd down to dwell in a land there where they used to grant protection, not to seek for it ;

[And the nearest tribes of 'Amir to us were 'Uqail in al-Miranah, and the Wibar.]

And the valley-bottoms were given, in exchange for Nurnair, the hoofs of steeds by which the dust was raised high in air.

And the tribe of the Sons of Kilab, though they fled, flight did not save them.

And Sulaim kept silence over their cud through fear of us, even as the ass keeps silence.

And as for Ashja' the man-woman, they turned tail like goats in ash-Shadha, bleating as they fled.

And we met not our deaths from Murrah, for they turned and took the road taken before them by Haribah, and went down into the lowland.

[Ancient glory and renown undimmed forbid the Sons of Khuzaimah to yield in aught :

[They excel all Ma'add in noble qualities, wheresoever they dwell, whithersoever they wend ;

[Faithful are they to their word when once it is pledged, and straight they turn to the gaming-arrows when men long for the smell of roast meat.]

Carry then a message, if thou touchest upon us in discourse, to Kinanah our brethren, wheresoever they be :

We take the place of those who have gone away, and we occupy at will the highest region of Najd when the rains fail [and famine comes],

With led mares, all pressing on, frisky, prancing out of the road in wantonness, made lean and spare by constant duty in places of danger and in distant raids,

Striving against the reins, unquiet as though in each of them there were a locust in a cloud of dust, yellow in colour,

Thrusting back with their elbows the girth, with the space between their teats stopped up with dust ;

Thou mayst see them gray from the sweat dried upon them — here a plentiful flow, there only a little ;

In every place of soft soil, wheresoever they wheeled about, is a well-liko footprint of the hoof with the sides crumbling in :

And with many a noble stallion the sheath of whose yard is like a folded wine-skin which the vintners have hung up on a peg :

The noise of his nostrils, when other horses cannot breathe freely, is like the working of a bellows borrowed from a blacksmith.

He is trained in the evenings, and is strong and sturdy, slender-waisted, tall on his legs, with no superfluous flesh.

What time other horses have their coats dishevelled and rough after a brisk gallop in the morning, his back is like a hard well-twisted cable.

All day, by the side of the riders on camels, he speeds swiftly along, the white blaze on his forehead looking like a woman's veil.

Yea, there will not save from disaster, when battle presses closely, aught but firm steadfastness in fight, or flight.

poems.title: Ode XCIX: To whom belong the dwellings thou
poems.author: Bishr ibn Abi Khazim
poems.text:
To whom belong the dwellings thou hast lighted on at al-An'um, the traces of which stand forth like the markings of a spotted snake ?

The East wind has played with them, and they have become unrecognizable, but for a remnant of their trench with its sides broken in.

They were the abode of a girl with white side-teeth, soft and tender, slender in the flanks, plump in the fore-arm where the bracelet goes round.

She listened to the talk of the tale-bearers about us, and has severed the bonds that bound her to thee, and gone with thy former partners on their road towards Syria ;

And thou hast become, from excess of longing and desire of love, stricken at heart like one smitten senseless.

Why dost thou not bring forgetfulness to thy grief with a strong she-camel, brisk as a wild ass, like a stallion-camel scarred with bites,

One that goes proudly with the saddle upon her, trustworthy in the night journey — one that slaps her thighs with her tail, and breaks the stones with her chipped hoof?

Ask Tamim of their wars with us, and 'Amir — and is the experienced like him who does not know ?

Tamlm were wroth because 'Amir were slaughtered on the day of an-Nisar : so they were brought in the end to calamity themselves.

Our wont was, when they shouted' loudly for war, to cure the fume in their heads with a band of warriors that shocked them hard ;

We batter the tops of their helmets with our swords, and we shout our names and our fathers', while our horses are marked about their throats with blood.

[Our steeds] come forth from the dust-cloud with bared teeth, dashing along like beasts of prey, mounted on each a warrior like a lion dusky brown of hue,

Warriors long in the baldric, that leap down to engage on foot, that long to reach their adversaries, not clipped in their claws !

So they broke their host, and Hajib fled away beneath the dust-cloud, enveloped in dusky mirk ;

And they saw their eagle, the triumphant, attacked by a lion, buff-coloured, sharp-clawed, mighty in his grip.

Aforetime our men slew Hujr — all' the spears were pointed at him, and prone he fell on his face :

He strives to rise — but into his body have passed the shafts of the spears, all pliant and supple, fitted with sharp spear-heads.

And the Sons of Numair — we have met of them cavalry whose gums watered for spoil :

But our riders came upon them unawares — every. prancing mare, and horse that in his bounds cuts through the girth-rings of the light saddle, battering the ground mightily with his hoofs.

And they trampled on the Sons of Kilab with a vehement trampling, and drove them to take refuge by the tent-poles of their camping-place.

And before that they brought disaster to Ka'b, with lances well straightened, which the hands ply nimbly to and fro,

Until we gave them to drink of a bitter cup, the sips of which were as nauseous to the taste as colocynth.
